#### Why the word has to be split before anything can be designed

**Start with the problem the word causes.** When someone says "we need streaming", they could mean any of five different things — an answer within a deadline, an answer soon, a job that never ends, work triggered per record, or a cheap approximate answer. Those are five different requirements. None of them is a statement about the engine.

**In this book "streaming" means one narrow thing:** an execution engine designed for **unbounded** data — a dataset with no end. That is all. It does not promise low latency, it does not imply approximation, and it is not the opposite of batch.

**Then the fact that makes it hard.** Every event carries two timestamps:

- **event time** — when the thing actually happened, stamped by whatever produced it.
- **processing time** — when the pipeline observed it, read off the pipeline's own clock.

They disagree, always, by an amount nobody controls. In this book's dataset event 7 happened at **12:00:50** and was seen at **12:04:40** — 230s apart. A phone was offline; a queue backed up. Nothing is broken.

**And that gap changes answers, not just timings.** Count the same 9 events per minute by event time and then by processing time: **3 of the 6 minutes get a different number.** The 12:00 minute is 12 by event time and 8 by processing time. No event was lost and no sum is miscalculated — the two columns are answering two different questions.

#### When each meaning of the word is the one you want

**You want the engine (this book's meaning) when your input has no end** — a click stream, a sensor feed, a log. The test is not "is it fast?" but "can I ever read to the end?" If you cannot, you need a model that says when to speak, because "when the input is finished" is not available.

**You want "real time" — a latency promise — when a human or a control loop is waiting.** That is a separate requirement, and you can satisfy it with a batch job on a tight schedule. Many systems called streaming are exactly that.

**You want "approximate" when the exact answer costs more than it is worth.** Also separate, also compatible with either engine.

**What this does not settle:** which clock your pipeline should bucket on. That is the next concept, and it is a question about your users' question, not about your infrastructure. The four questions the book is built on — **what** is computed, **where** in event time, **when** results are materialized, **how** refinements relate — exist precisely to keep those decisions apart. Only "when" is about processing time.

#### Visual walkthrough — one word, two clocks, two answers

The animation loops through all 4 steps. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch01-terminology/ch01-terminology.svg" alt="Visual walkthrough — one word, two clocks, two answers, 4 animated steps" width="1040">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — the word "streaming" means five different things</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch01-terminology/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: the word &quot;streaming&quot; means five different things" width="1040">

Five of these six describe a property someone wants from the ANSWER — how fast it comes, how often, how exact. Only the last describes the SYSTEM. Mixing the two is why "do we need streaming?" is a question two engineers can answer differently while agreeing on every fact.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — every event carries TWO timestamps, and they disagree</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch01-terminology/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: every event carries TWO timestamps, and they disagree" width="1040">

Read the two times on any row and they differ. Read event 7 and they differ by 230s — it happened in the first minute and arrived in the fifth. Every difficulty in this book follows from that one gap, so the dataset is built to contain it rather than to be tidy.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — count by the wrong clock and the answer changes</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch01-terminology/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: count by the wrong clock and the answer changes" width="1040">

This is the whole problem in one table. Bucketing by processing time says the 12:00 minute saw 8; bucketing by event time says 12. 3 of 6 minutes disagree. A processing-time dashboard is not a slightly-stale event-time dashboard — it answers a different question and can be arbitrarily far off.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — so the book asks four questions of every pipeline</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch01-terminology/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: so the book asks four questions of every pipeline" width="1040">

These four are not a summary — they are the book's actual structure, and the reason the previous step's table has two columns. WHERE picks the event-time slice; WHEN picks the processing-time moment to speak. A system that only has "when" is a processing-time dashboard, which is the thing that was 33% low.

</details>
